questions.topic: What a resource-exhaustion attack actually takes away
questions.learningObjective: Identify the resource that an exhaustion attack consumes
questions.stem: A reviewer claims the platform is unavailable because an attacker exhausted server memory, and asks the team to add redundant servers before reviewing the code.

options.text: The exhausted resource is server memory, so adding machines leaves the vulnerable code path in place
The exhausted resource is network bandwidth, so extra machines would spread the same traffic faster
options.misconception: assumes the exhausted resource is bandwidth rather than memory

options.text: The exhausted resource is disk space, so the fix is to rotate old log files on a fixed schedule
options.misconception: assumes the exhausted resource is disk space rather than memory

options.text: The attacker must have stolen credentials, so the fix is to require multi-factor authentication
options.misconception: treats an exhaustion attack as a credential theft incident

questions.explanation: Memory is the named exhausted resource, so scaling out leaves the flaw untouched. The other readings misidentify the resource or invent a credential-theft cause.
questions.hint: Name the resource the brief says ran out.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a reflection attack works only when the source address can be chosen
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the source address decides where reflected traffic lands
questions.stem: An operator asks why an amplification path that reflects traffic to a third party cannot be used against a server whose source address cannot be chosen.

options.text: Because reflection always requires the reflector to answer the forged request at the same rate
options.misconception: thinks the reflector must answer at the same rate

options.text: Because the reflected traffic is sent to the forged source, so it reaches the victim only if that address can be chosen
Because reflection attacks require the third party to consent to the request before responding
options.misconception: believes third-party consent is the deciding factor

options.text: Because forged source addresses are always dropped before the request reaches the reflector
options.misconception: assumes forged packets are always dropped in transit

options.text: The link carried 420 percent of its capacity, so the attacker must have succeeded completely
options.misconception: reads an overloaded link as proof the attack succeeded

options.text: The site can absorb the attack because its outbound capacity exceeds the inbound link capacity
options.misconception: confuses outbound capacity with inbound capacity

The gap between inbound and outbound capacity shows spare capacity the site can use for flooding
options.misconception: treats unused outbound capacity as usable inbound headroom

questions.explanation: The attack traffic is 4.2 gigabits against a 1 gigabit link, roughly four times what the link carries. Outbound capacity is irrelevant here because the flood arrives on the inbound side.
questions.hint: Compare the arriving rate with the inbound link rate.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the accept queue and the connection table each bound
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the accept queue from the connection table
questions.stem: Explain the difference between the accept queue and the connection table to a colleague who thinks they are two names for the same list.

answer.exemplar: The accept queue holds connections that have completed the TCP handshake but have not yet been accepted by the application, so it bounds how many finished handshakes wait for a worker. The connection table holds the state of every connection the host is tracking, including ones still mid-handshake, so it consumes memory and is what a flood of half-open connections exhausts.

questions.explanation: The accept queue holds finished connections waiting for the application, while the connection table holds every tracked connection including half-open ones. Incomplete handshakes never reach the queue.
questions.hint: Ask which one is charged before the handshake completes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a value in the handshake buys and what it costs the server
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a signed timestamp protects and what it costs

stimulus.body: A public API requires clients to send a signed timestamp header with each request. The server records the last timestamp it accepted and rejects anything older than five minutes or more than thirty seconds ahead of its own clock. About two thousand requests arrive each second and each accepted request costs the server roughly forty milliseconds of work.

questions.stem: Using the design brief, identify what the signed timestamp buys the server and what it costs it.

options.text: It stops replay outright, because any copied request will be rejected once its timestamp ages
options.misconception: believes the timestamp check alone stops every replay

options.text: It removes the need for server state, because the client supplies the freshness value
options.misconception: assumes a client-supplied time removes all server state

options.text: It guarantees ordering, so duplicate deliveries disappear along with stale requests
options.misconception: confuses freshness with ordering and exactly-once delivery

options.text: It bounds how long a captured request stays usable, and it costs a comparison per request

questions.explanation: The timestamp only makes a captured request useless once it ages past the window; it does not stop copies sent inside that window. The server also pays a comparison and one stored timestamp per request.
questions.hint: Ask how long a captured request remains acceptable.

options.misconception: assumes flow tracking state is written to disk

options.text: Tracking consumes processor cycles only, so a faster gateway holds more flows with no penalty
options.misconception: believes faster processors remove flow-table pressure

questions.explanation: First the table is the target; then the allocation rule points to gateway memory. Because flow records live in memory, a flood of distinct flows exhausts the gateway itself.

options.misconception: blames a shared token array for the unused bucket

options.text: The bucket is unused because the refill timer is scheduled on the wrong thread
options.misconception: blames timer scheduling for the unused bucket

options.misconception: invents a cache warm-up requirement

options.text: The bucket is unused because the decision path reads the counter and skips the token check entirely

questions.explanation: The limiter asks the fixed counter instead of the bucket, so stored tokens never apply and bursts are rejected at the refill rate. The fix is to consult the bucket state in the decision path.

options.misconception: ties attack origin to network position

options.misconception: blames reflector discards instead of forged addresses

options.text: The reflector answered 380 requests, because 620 replies arrived at the wrong address
options.misconception: reads the delivered count as the unanswered count

options.text: The reflector answered all 1000 requests, but 380 replies were delivered to addresses the tester did not own
The reflector answered 1000 requests and the test shows the forge is 62 percent effective
options.misconception: treats delivery to the tester as the only useful outcome

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a volumetric attack costs the two sides differently
questions.learningObjective: Compare the costs borne by the buyer and the target of a flood
questions.stem: Explain why the attacker and the target of a large flood experience the same packets in very different ways.

answer.exemplar: The attacker's cost is metered bandwidth, which they choose to buy in advance and stop buying when they stop paying, while the target's cost is the capacity that good customers needed: the link carrying attack traffic, the server processing it, and the revenue lost while legitimate requests queue. The same megabytes are a cheap commodity to the buyer and an expensive loss to the seller, which is why a small purchase of traffic can threaten a large business.

questions.explanation: The buyer pays a metered price and can stop; the seller loses the capacity and the business behind it. Identical packets with opposite incentives make the attack cheap and the damage large.
questions.hint: Compare what each side pays for and what each loses.

options.text: The limit works per address, so one customer reaching it from many addresses still takes most slots
The limit works as intended, because no single address may hold more than 200 connections
options.misconception: ignores that the customer controls many addresses

options.text: The limit is ineffective, because 200 connections is far below what the service can serve overall
options.misconception: compares the per-address cap with total service capacity

options.text: The limit is ineffective, because the service never closes connections that are already open
options.misconception: assumes the cap should retire existing open connections

questions.topic: What a value in the handshake buys and what it costs the server
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a per-account counter prevents and what it costs
questions.stem: A service requires clients to send a monotonically increasing counter that the server remembers per account, and the team asks what that buys and what it costs.

options.text: It proves the client's identity, because only a named account can produce a rising counter
options.misconception: treats a per-account counter as an identity proof

options.text: It stops a captured request being replayed after the window closes, and it costs server state per account
It guarantees exactly-once delivery, because a repeated counter value can never be processed twice
options.misconception: confuses duplicate suppression with exactly-once delivery

options.text: It removes the need for rate limiting, because a rising counter bounds the request rate
options.misconception: believes a monotonic counter bounds request rate

options.misconception: dismisses the per-packet insert as harmless

options.text: The bug is in the table size, because 4096 entries is too small for any modern gateway

The bug affects only logging, because the flow table is also used as the audit log
options.misconception: claims the flow table doubles as an audit log

options.text: The counter is stricter, because it caps the rate exactly even for a burst inside one minute
options.misconception: believes a fixed counter smooths bursts better

options.text: The two are identical, because both limit long-run throughput to the same number

options.text: The service is losing service, because the queue grows faster than it drains and the processor is saturated

options.misconception: blames ordinary demand for the drop in throughput

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a reflection attack works only when the source address can be chosen
questions.learningObjective: Explain why choosing the forged source address is essential to reflection
questions.stem: Ask the team to explain why choosing the forged source address is the part of a reflection attack that cannot be skipped.

answer.exemplar: A reflection attack borrows someone else's bandwidth: the attacker sends a small request to an open service with the victim's address written into it, and the service's much larger answer is delivered to the victim. Every step of that chain is fixed except the address, so if the attacker cannot choose the source address the answer lands on the attacker's own host, the victim never feels the traffic, and the amplification has no target to spend on.

questions.explanation: The answer follows the source address in the request, so the address decides who pays. Without a chosen address the amplified traffic returns to the attacker and no third party is harmed.
questions.hint: Ask where the amplified answer is delivered.

options.text: In the accept queue, because it was configured for only 512 entries
options.misconception: blames the accept queue for the refusals

options.text: In the tracking table, because 65536 entries was too few for the flood
options.misconception: blames the tracking table limit for the refusals

questions.topic: What a resource-exhaustion attack actually takes away
questions.learningObjective: Explain why exhaustion attacks do not need to break cryptography
questions.stem: Explain to a non-specialist why exhausting a resource is the goal of an attack that never breaks the cryptography.

answer.exemplar: An attacker does not need to defeat the mathematics if the server runs out of memory, file descriptors, worker threads, or bandwidth while trying to answer. questions.explanation: Exhaustion works on quantity, not on breaking cryptography: replies stay correct but the machine cannot finish them. Expecting a cryptographic weakness misses the mechanism entirely.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence the decisions needed before changing rate limiting
questions.stem: A service team wants to replace a fixed window counter with a token bucket and asks what must be decided before the change is safe.

options.text: Decide the refill rate first, because it sets the sustained throughput of the service
options.misconception: treats the rate as the only decision that matters

options.text: Decide the bucket capacity first, because it sets the total work the service can do
options.misconception: treats capacity as the only decision that matters

options.text: Decide both the capacity and the refill rate, because each controls a different failure mode
Decide the storage location first, because the counters must live in a shared database
options.misconception: reduces the change to where the counters are stored

questions.explanation: First, the refill rate sets the sustained rate; second, the capacity sets the worst-case burst. Choosing only one leaves the other failure mode open.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two numbers controls.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a resource-exhaustion attack actually takes away
questions.learningObjective: Identify which resource a flood of tiny packets exhausts
questions.stem: A ticket claims the outage came from an attacker sending enormous numbers of tiny packets so the server spent all its time on headers.

options.text: The described attack exhausts processor time and memory, so the fix is to cap work per connection
The described attack exhausts disk space, so the fix is to rotate the log files more often
options.misconception: reads a header-processing flood as a disk exhaustion

options.text: The described attack exhausts bandwidth, so the fix is to request a larger pipe from the provider
options.misconception: assumes every volumetric attack is purely a bandwidth problem

options.text: The described attack steals session cookies, so the fix is to rotate the signing key
options.misconception: confuses a flood with credential compromise

questions.explanation: Tiny packets force far more header parsing than the bytes delivered, so processor time and memory run out. Bandwidth and disk are not the binding constraints here.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the work the packet count multiplies.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a reflection attack works only when the source address can be chosen
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limit on reflection from an unspoofable source
questions.stem: During an incident review, an analyst wants to explain precisely what stops a reflection attack being launched from a host whose outbound source address cannot be set.

options.text: The target's return path is already saturated, so extra reflected packets cannot add load
options.misconception: blames return-path saturation rather than address choice

options.text: The reflected packets are delivered to the forged source, so they only harm a victim the attacker can name
The reflector refuses to answer packets whose source it cannot resolve to a live host
options.misconception: invents a reflector-side reverse lookup requirement

options.text: The attack needs the target to answer first, which the reflection technique never requires
options.misconception: claims the target must respond before reflection works

questions.explanation: The whole technique depends on sending the answer to a chosen address, so a host that cannot choose its source sends the amplified traffic home. Address choice, not path saturation, is the limit.
questions.hint: Ask where the amplified answer is delivered.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a volumetric attack costs the two sides differently
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the fraction of demand served during a flood
questions.stem: During a 60 minute flood a site handled 1.2 million requests normally while the attacker sent 900 million, and the server answered 45000 requests per minute at peak.

options.text: The site absorbed the flood, because 1.2 million requests is more than the attacker's total
options.misconception: compares normal traffic totals against attack packet totals

options.text: The site was fully available, because 1.2 million successful requests proves nothing was lost
options.misconception: reads surviving request counts as proof of full availability

options.text: The attacker's 900 million requests were all discarded, so the site lost no capacity at all
options.misconception: assumes all attack traffic was discarded before costing capacity

options.text: The site served about 2.7 million of 901 million requests, so roughly 99.7 percent was refused

questions.explanation: At 45000 per minute for an hour the site served about 2.7 million of 901 million requests, so roughly 99.7 percent was refused. Availability was a fraction of demand.
questions.hint: Compute the served total and compare it with demand.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the accept queue and the connection table each bound
questions.learningObjective: Explain why table exhaustion recovers more slowly than queue exhaustion
questions.stem: Ask the team to explain why a flood that exhausts the connection table is harder to recover from than one that exhausts the accept queue.

answer.exemplar: The accept queue holds only connections that have already completed their handshake, so when it overflows the server has finished the expensive part of the work and only needs to shed waiting entries. The connection table holds every tracked connection including half-open ones, and those entries are only released when their handshake times out, so the server stays in the overloaded state for the whole timeout period after the flood stops. Recovery is therefore bounded by the timeout rather than by the arrival of traffic.

questions.explanation: A queue overflow clears as soon as the application catches up, but table entries persist until their handshake times out. The recovery delay is set by the timeout, not the traffic.
questions.hint: Ask how long each kind of entry survives after traffic stops.
